treatments.frequency: Start with three to four visits a week; advance exercises and demonstrate evidence of functional improvement. Quickly advance to inclusion of strengthening exercises, aerobic exercises, mirror or image therapy or other functional exercise. Simultaneous home exercise prescription. Transition to home-based exercise program.

treatments.treatment: Mirror Therapy and Guided Imagery for CRPS
treatments.brief: - for motivated patients with moderate and severe CRPS who are willing to comply with the treatment.
treatments.indications: 1) Moderate and severe cases of complex regional pain syndrome, 2) May be helpful for those having difficulty complying with progressive strengthening exercises
treatments.frequency: Home exercises requiring an estimated ten minutes of each waking hour for six weeks. Best results obtained from viewing unaffected limb and performing activities as fast and accurately as possible with affected hand. Clinic appointments at least three times a week for six weeks in addition to home exercises. Additional treatments in two to three week increments provided continuing objective evidence of improvement.

treatments.brief: - for patients with CRPS to develop increasing tolerance to graded activities.
treatments.indications: 1) Moderate to severe CRPS, 2) Underlying morbidity making weight bearing problematic, 3) Lower extremity CRPS severe with weight bearing difficulty
treatments.frequency: Appointments initially three times a week, but five times a week if severe CRPS. Home exercises should be simultaneously prescribed.

treatments.brief: - for the treatment of CRPS.
treatments.indications: 1) Moderate to severe complex regional pain syndrome with significant hyperalgesia, 2) Should be primarily engaged in a core program of graded strengthening exercises
treatments.frequency: Appointments initially three times a week, but five times a week if severe CRPS. Home exercises should be simultaneously prescribed.

treatments.brief: - for treatment of CRPS.
treatments.indications: 1) Moderate to severe complex regional pain syndrome patients, 2) Particularly indicated for those who are motivated and interested in yoga
treatments.frequency: Dose/Duration: Appointments initially three times a week, but five times a week if severe CRPS. Daily home exercises should be simultaneously prescribed. J.
treatments.duration: Appointments initially three times a week, but five times a week if severe CRPS. Daily home exercises should be simultaneously prescribed. J.

treatments.brief: - for the treatment of CRPS.
treatments.indications: 1) CRPS sufficiently severe to require medications, 2) Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs as adjunct to strengthening and aerobic exercise, 3) Cyclooxygenase-2 selective preferred as first-line
treatments.frequency: For most patients, scheduled dosage rather than as needed is preferred. Prescribing nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs as needed is reasonable for mild or moderate symptoms. Due to potential adverse effects from chronic use (more than two months), patients should be periodically monitored for hypertension, blood loss, renal insufficiency, and hepatic enzyme elevations.
treatments.duration: Per pain course; discontinue upon resolution, lack of efficacy, or adverse effects

treatments.brief: - for treatment of CRPS, particularly if NSAIDs are contraindicated.
treatments.indications: 1) CRPS sufficiently severe to require medications, 2) Acetaminophen as adjunct to strengthening and aerobic exercise, 3) Preferred over older nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs as first-line
treatments.frequency: Generally prescribed up to 3.5g/day in divided doses, usually four times a day dosing.
treatments.duration: Per pain course; discontinue upon resolution or adverse effects

treatments.brief: - as intravenous adjuncts for regional blockades that also include lidocaine and clonidine for treatment of CRPS.
treatments.indications: 1) Severe complex regional pain syndrome that has responded insufficiently to progressive strengthening exercises, aerobic exercises, and oral medications including bisphosphonates

treatments.treatment: Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibitor Anti-depressants for CRPS
treatments.brief: - tricyclic anti-depressants (includes norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor anti-depressants) for treatment of CRPS.
treatments.indications: 1) Complex regional pain syndrome patients with sleep disruption and mild dysthymia, which may respond to serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors
treatments.frequency: Prescribe at a low dose at night and gradually increase (e.g., amitriptyline 25mg QHS, increase by 25mg each week) until sub-maximal or maximal dose is achieved, sufficient effects are achieved, or adverse effects occur. Generally, lower doses (e.g., amitriptyline 25 to 75mg/day) to avoid adverse effects. For CRPS, duration may be indefinite, although most patients do not require it as the condition usually improves or resolves. Imipramine is less sedating if there is carryover daytime sedation.
treatments.duration: Per clinical response; ongoing while effective

treatments.brief: - a trial of duloxetine for treatment of CRPS after attempting other treatments (e.g., strengthening exercises, aerobic exercise, bisphosphonates) and if TCAs are not tolerated, and if treatment efficacy can be documented.
treatments.indications: 1) CRPS sufficient to require medications, 2) Failed multiple modalities: progressive strengthening, aerobic exercise, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, tricyclic antidepressants, anticonvulsants
treatments.frequency: 60mg daily. There appears to be either a minimal or no advantage of twice daily dosing over 60mg daily. Duration for CRPS pain may be indefinitely, although some patients do not require it if compliant with functional restoration program.
treatments.duration: Per clinical response; ongoing while effective

treatments.brief: - for treatment of severe CRPS is selectively
treatments.indications: 1) Generally not indicated; consideration for severe chronic CRPS as fourth- or fifth-line, 2) After progressive strengthening, aerobic exercises, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
treatments.frequency: Frequency and dosing per manufacturer. Duration for CRPS patients may be indefinitely, although most do not require indefinite treatment as the condition usually improves or resolves spontaneously.

treatments.brief: - for treatment of moderate to severe CRPS if other therapies have proven insufficient to control symptoms.
treatments.indications: 1) CRPS with unsuccessful symptom control including strengthening, aerobic exercise, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, bisphosphonates, clonidine, and tricyclic antidepressants, 2) Short-term use
treatments.frequency: One suggested regimen: gabapentin 600mg daily for two days, then 600mg twice daily for two days, then 600mg three times a day for days five to 21. Dose escalation should be cautiously done. Duration usually limited as most patients do not require indefinite treatment. Efficacy labeled as 'mild' and quality evidence suggests benefits are short-term.
treatments.duration: Short-term only; taper as symptoms improve

treatments.brief: - for patients with CRPS after physical therapy interventions have been trialed.
treatments.indications: 1) Moderate or severe complex regional pain syndrome, including in acute to subacute as well as chronic phases, 2) Should be included as part of functional restoration plan where strengthening, aerobic, and other functional exercises are central
treatments.frequency: Taken in oral or parenteral formulations. Recommended regimens include: Alendronate 40mg daily for eight weeks; Clodronate 300mg IV daily for ten days; Alendronate 7.5mg IV daily for three days; Pamidronate 60mg IV for one dose; Neridronate 100mg IV every ten days for 40 days. Duration for oral treatment may be indefinite, although most do not require it as the condition usually gradually improves or resolves.
treatments.duration: Per clinical response; ongoing while effective

treatments.brief: - as a treatment option for CRPS patients.
treatments.indications: 1) Severe CRPS with inadequate relief from strengthening, aerobic exercise, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, corticosteroids, tricyclic antidepressants, therapy, and bisphosphonates
treatments.frequency: Dosing: intranasal calcitonin 100IU three times a day for three weeks, 400IU daily for four weeks, and 200 IU daily plus calcium 500mg a day. Duration may be indefinite, although most do not require this as the condition usually improves or resolves spontaneously.
treatments.duration: Per clinical response; ongoing while effective

treatments.brief: - administered by oral or regional blockade for treatment of moderately severe CRPS that is not responsive to rehabilitative therapy, NSAIDs, tricyclic anti-depressants, or glucocorticosteroids.
treatments.indications: 1) Severe complex regional pain syndrome that is not responsive to strengthening exercises, aerobic exercise, other exercise, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, bisphosphonates, tricyclic antidepressants, and glucocorticosteroids
treatments.frequency: Three injections at weekly intervals. The single quality study used: 30 micrograms clonidine plus 1 milligram per kilogram lidocaine plus 0.9% saline solution plus 5 milligrams parecoxib. As parecoxib is not available in the United States, other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs could be considered.

treatments.treatment: Intravenous Regional Anesthesia with Clonidine for Preventive
treatments.brief: - for administration prior to surgery to prevent recurrence of CRPS in patients who have previously had CRPS.
treatments.indications: 1) Patients undergoing surgery who have a prior history of complex regional pain syndrome, 2) May be considered for those at high risk for complex regional pain syndrome
treatments.frequency: Transdermal patch or oral per dosing guidelines
treatments.duration: Trial period 2-4 weeks; continue if beneficial

treatments.brief: - for short-term treatment of CRPS.
treatments.indications: 1) Moderate to severe CRPS insufficiently controlled with progressive strengthening, aerobic exercise, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, 2) Bisphosphonates also reasonable at this stage
treatments.frequency: One regimen: Prednisolone 40mg orally daily for 14 days then 10mg/week taper. Second regimen: prednisone 10mg orally three times a day for up to 12 weeks. No comparative evidence to suggest which is superior. If significant improvement, continue for additional two months. Subsequent treatment individualized based on ongoing improvements and risk/benefit of continued glucocorticosteroid therapy.

treatments.frequency: As needed per manufacturer recommendations; over-the-counter agents preferred first-line.

treatments.treatment: NSAIDs - Gastrointestinal Protection for Hand/Finger Osteoarthrosis
treatments.brief: - Concurrent use of cytoprotective drugs (misoprostol, sucralfate, H2 blockers, proton pump inhibitors) for patients at high-risk of GI bleeding on NSAIDs.
treatments.indications: 1) high-risk factor profile who also have indications for nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, 2) At-risk patients: history prior gastrointestinal bleeding, elderly, diabetics, cigarette smokers
treatments.duration: Concurrent with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use

treatments.treatment: NSAIDs - Cardiovascular Risk Management for Hand/Finger Osteoarthrosis
treatments.brief: - Acetaminophen or aspirin as first-line therapy for patients at cardiovascular risk; if needed, non-selective NSAIDs preferred over COX-2 drugs.
treatments.indications: 1) Known cardiovascular disease or multiple risk factors, 2) Acetaminophen or aspirin as safest first-line, 3) Non-selective nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs preferred over cyclooxygenase-2

treatments.brief: - Recommended for acute flares or chronic hand osteoarthrosis.
treatments.indications: 1) acute flares or chronic hand osteoarthritis, 2) Indicated when symptoms insufficiently treated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, acetaminophen, and/or topical medications
treatments.duration: Per clinical response; ongoing for chronic management.

treatments.brief: - Active therapy recommended for treatment of hand/finger osteoarthrosis.
treatments.indications: 1) treatment of acute flares or chronic hand osteoarthritis, 2) Goals: grip/pinch strength, range of motion, pain management

treatments.brief: - Recommended for treatment of Hand/Finger Osteoarthrosis. Functional goals: grip/pinch strength, range of motion, return to work.
treatments.indications: 1) post-operative and recovery phase treatment of Hand/Finger osteoarthritis, 2) Exercise not indicated acutely; indicated when functional deficits exist, 3) Goals: increased grip strength, key pinch, range of motion, work capacity
treatments.duration: 2-3 visits for mild deficits; up to 12-15 for severe deficits with documented functional improvement.

treatments.treatment: Self-Application of Ice for Hand/Finger Osteoarthrosis
treatments.brief: - Self-application of ice recommended for treatment of Hand/Finger Osteoarthrosis.
treatments.indications: 1) treatment of Hand/Finger osteoarthritis. Typically used for acute/subacute symptoms relief
treatments.frequency: 15-20 minutes, 3-5 times daily or as needed.

treatments.treatment: Self-Application of Heat for Hand/Finger Osteoarthrosis
treatments.brief: - Self-application of heat recommended for treatment of Hand/Finger Osteoarthrosis.
treatments.indications: 1) treatment of Hand/Finger osteoarthritis. Typically used for subacute or chronic pain relief

treatments.brief: - Recommended in select cases where hardware has been placed and subsequent hardware removal is indicated per doctor/patient preference.
treatments.indications: 1) recommended per doctor/patient preference where there is: (a) protruding hardware, (b) pain attributed to the hardware, (c) broken hardware on imaging, and/or (d) positive anesthetic injection response

treatments.treatment: NSAIDs for Treatment of Dupuytren's Disease
treatments.brief: - Recommended for treatment of acute, subacute, or chronic Dupuytren's Disease. OTC agents may suffice and should be tried first.
treatments.indications: 1) Acute, subacute, or chronic Dupuytren's disease, 2) As needed for symptom management, 3) Duration limited to shortest effective period
treatments.frequency: As needed per manufacturer recommendations; over-the-counter agents preferred first-line.

treatments.treatment: NSAIDs - Gastrointestinal Protection for Dupuytren's Disease
treatments.brief: - Concurrent use of cytoprotective drugs (misoprostol, sucralfate, H2 blockers, proton pump inhibitors) for patients at high-risk of GI bleeding on NSAIDs.
treatments.indications: 1) high-risk factor profile who also have indications for nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, 2) At-risk patients: history prior gastrointestinal bleeding, elderly, diabetics, cigarette smokers
treatments.duration: Concurrent with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use

treatments.treatment: NSAIDs - Cardiovascular Risk Management for Dupuytren's Disease
treatments.brief: - Acetaminophen or aspirin as first-line therapy for patients at cardiovascular risk; if needed, non-selective NSAIDs preferred over COX-2 drugs.
treatments.indications: 1) Known cardiovascular disease or multiple risk factors, 2) Acetaminophen or aspirin as safest first-line, 3) Non-selective nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs preferred over cyclooxygenase-2

treatments.treatment: Opioids for Acute/Post-operative Pain - Dupuytren's Disease
treatments.brief: - Recommended for limited use (<7 days) for acute and post-operative pain management as adjunctive therapy for Dupuytren's Disease.
treatments.indications: 1) Acute injury and post-operative pain, brief prescription as adjunct to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen, 2) Nocturnally preferred, 3) Documentation of compliance required
treatments.duration: Less than 7 days for acute; not more than 7 days for post-operative.

treatments.brief: - Recommended as part of the evaluation and management of patients with chronic pain to identify psychosocial barriers contributing to disability and inhibiting function.
treatments.indications: 1) Moderate to severe CRPS in certain clinical circumstances, 2) To assess whether psychological factors need to be considered and treated as part of the overall treatment plan, 3) See Behavioral Interventions section for full indications
treatments.frequency: As needed for initial evaluation and periodic reassessment.

treatments.treatment: Local Anesthetic Injections for Diagnosing CRPS
treatments.brief: - Selectively recommended for evaluations in CRPS patients with chronic persistent pain in a specific nerve distribution otherwise unexplained by other investigation.
treatments.indications: 1) Chronic persistent pain in a specific nerve distribution (e.g., ilioinguinal, genitofemoral) that is otherwise unexplained by other investigation, including imaging, electrodiagnostic/NCS, 2) Benefits: identify treatable lesion; adverse effects:

treatments.brief: - Recommended for the treatment of CRPS. All CRPS patients.
treatments.indications: 1) All CRPS patients, 2) Most severe CRPS patients require daily treatment at first to encourage increased activity, progress exercises, and address fear avoidant beliefs (kinesiophobia), 3) Mild to moderate cases: 2-3 times per week
treatments.frequency: 3-5 visits per week initially; severe cases may require daily treatment.
treatments.duration: Per clinical progress; duration based on functional improvement.

treatments.treatment: Vitamin C for Prevention of CRPS After Fractures
treatments.brief: - Recommended for the prevention/treatment of CRPS in select patients with fractures of the distal radius, wrist, hand, ankle, and foot.
treatments.indications: 1) Select patients with fractures of the distal radius, wrist, hand, ankle, and foot who are at risk for or developing CRPS, 2) Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) 500mg daily for 50 days has been studied for CRPS prevention post-fracture
treatments.frequency: 500mg daily (typical dose studied); per treating physician.

treatments.treatment: Open Sympathectomy and External Radiation for Sympathetic Blockade
treatments.brief: - Not Recommended for the treatment of CRPS.
treatments.indications: 1) Not recommended for the treatment of CRPS; Open sympathectomy and external radiation for sympathetic blockade are not supported by evidence

treatments.brief: - Recommended as part of evaluation and management of patients with chronic pain to identify psychosocial barriers contributing to disability.
treatments.indications: 1) Moderate to severe CRPS in which significant psychosocial dysfunction is observed or suspected, 2) Cases where psychological factors need to be considered in the overall treatment plan, 3) To assess readiness for and guide behavioral/
treatments.frequency: As needed; typically at treatment planning stages and periodic reassessment.

treatments.brief: - Recommended for select CRPS patients who have been treated with and are compliant with aerobic and strengthening exercises, NSAIDs, etc., with ongoing significant impairment.
treatments.indications: 1) CRPS pts treated and compliant with aerobic and strengthening exercises, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, etc., with ongoing significant impairment needing multidisciplinary rehabilitation
treatments.frequency: Typically as part of a multidisciplinary pain rehabilitation program.
treatments.duration: Per clinical progress and program structure.

treatments.brief: - Recommended for individuals presenting with a positive screen and/or signs and symptoms consistent with acute stress disorder or post-traumatic stress disorder.
treatments.indications: 1) Assist mental health providers in confirming acute stress disorder or post-traumatic stress disorder diagnosis, 2) Requires professionally trained mental health professional
treatments.frequency: One-time test battery administration; repeat as clinically indicated.

treatments.treatment: Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) for PTSD
treatments.brief: - Recommended for the treatment of patients with PTSD. EMDR includes multiple therapies including cognitive behavioral therapy and exposure therapy components.
treatments.indications: 1) For treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder, 2) Includes co-interventions such as cognitive behavioral therapy and exposure therapy, 3) Administered by trained mental health professional
treatments.frequency: Typically 8-12 sessions; per treating provider and clinical response.
treatments.duration: Per clinical response; evidence supports treatment completion over sufficient number of sessions.

treatments.treatment: Mind/Body Interventions: Guided Imagery for PTSD
treatments.brief: - Recommended for the treatment of patients with PTSD.
treatments.indications: 1) the treatment of patients with PTSD, 2) Mind/body interventions including guided imagery used as adjunctive treatment
treatments.frequency: Per treating provider; typically integrated into broader treatment program.

treatments.brief: - Not Recommended in the treatment of patients with PTSD.
treatments.indications: 1) Not recommended in the treatment of patients with PTSD

treatments.brief: - Not Recommended in the treatment of patients with PTSD.
treatments.indications: 1) Not recommended in the treatment of patients with PTSD

treatments.brief: - Surgical/Operative procedures for TBI are at the discretion of the physician based on clinical assessment, evaluation, and clinical judgment.
treatments.indications: 1) Procedures are at the discretion of the physician based on clinical assessment/evaluation and clinical judgment. 2) Surgical intervention indicated based on severity of injury, presence of hematoma, increased intracranial pressure

treatments.treatment: NSAIDs for Musculoskeletal Pain/Fever Associated with TBI
treatments.brief: - Recommended for treatment of musculoskeletal pain and fever control associated with TBI. PPIs, H2 blockers, or sucralfate may be added to reduce GI risk.
treatments.indications: 1) Musculoskeletal pain and fever control associated with traumatic brain injury, 2) Proton pump inhibitors or histamine blockers with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs to reduce ulceration risk

treatments.treatment: Acetaminophen for Musculoskeletal Pain/Fever Associated with TBI
treatments.brief: - Recommended for treatment of musculoskeletal pain and fever control associated with TBI, particularly in patients with contraindications for NSAIDs.
treatments.indications: 1) musculoskeletal pain and fever control associated with TBI, for patients with contraindications for nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, 2) Per manufacturer's recommendations
treatments.duration: Resolution of symptoms or development of adverse effects.

treatments.treatment: Topical Drug Delivery for Post-TBI Musculoskeletal Pain
treatments.brief: - Recommended for post-TBI musculoskeletal pain in select patients who cannot tolerate oral medications or prefer topical treatments.
treatments.indications: 1) Topical drug delivery including capsaicin, topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and topical salicylates for post-traumatic brain injury pain, 2) For patients who cannot tolerate oral medications

treatments.treatment: Antidepressants for TBI Patients with Depression
treatments.brief: - Recommended for treatment of TBI patients with depressive symptoms or depression.
treatments.indications: 1) depression in TBI patients, 2) Evidence supports use of antidepressants for depressive symptoms following TBI
treatments.frequency: Per treating physician and manufacturer recommendations.
treatments.duration: Per clinical response; typically continued for at least 6-12 months post-remission.

treatments.brief: - Recommended for treatment of TBI patients. Indications include tachycardia management, hypertension, paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity, and agitation.
treatments.indications: 1) management of tachycardia in TBI patients, 2) May be used as an option for hypertensive management, 3) May also be used to treat paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity or agitation, 4) Frequency/Dose/Duration: Per manufacturer's recommendations

treatments.brief: - Recommended in the treatment of select patients with traumatic hyphema.
treatments.indications: 1) the treatment of select patients with traumatic hyphema, 2) Rigid shield used to protect the injured eye from further trauma
treatments.duration: Per clinical course of hyphema resolution.

treatments.brief: - Not Recommended for inflamed pterygia or pingueculae.
treatments.indications: 1) Not recommended for inflamed pterygia or pingueculae; Glucocorticosteroid drops are preferred for inflamed pterygia/pingueculae when artificial tears alone are insufficient
